canberra.title: Godzilla Minus Zero proves Japanese cinema does the iconic lizard best
canberra.snippet: If the most recent two Japanese Godzilla films have taught Western audiences anything, it’s that more international films deserve t...
canberra.content:
Godzilla Minus Zero is the 34th monster movie by Toho Co. Photo: Toho Studios.

If the most recent two Japanese Godzilla films have taught Western audiences anything, it’s that more international films deserve to be seen on the big screen.

Godzilla has been around for over 80 years. It has appeared in 39 films (Japanese and American combined), yet despite the radioactive lizard’s consistent presence, he still wows audiences worldwide.

While the American films have left a bit to be desired, Japanese studio Toho keeps making banger after banger.

Their newest film, Godzilla Minus Zero, a direct sequel to 2023’s Minus One, continues this trend and leaves behind a very important question: How does Hollywood keep dropping the ball when making movies about giant monsters?

Minus Zero continues where Minus One left off. It’s 1949, and Japan is still dealing with the fallout of World War II and the Godzilla attack on Tokyo only a couple of years prior.

Former kamikaze pilot Kōichi (Ryunosuke Kamiki) has married Noriko (Minami Hamabe), who survived Godzilla’s attack on Tokyo in the previous film. The pair live with their adopted daughter and war orphan Akiko (Sae Nagatani).

Kōichi and Noriko are called back to action when a new monster, believed to have landed in Japan via a meteor, begins to destroy villages across the country.

The pair joins their former colleague, Dr Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka), whom they helped defeat Godzilla, now the director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau.

Alongside new characters, including meteorologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa) and Hiroshima survivor Kanji (Min Tanaka), the group must defeat this new monster before it causes further devastation while also keeping an eye on Godzilla’s remains.

Spoilers: he’s not dead. It is called Godzilla after all.

In December 2023, Region published a review for Godzilla Minus One, and in that review the film was praised for its superb cast of human characters, a surprisingly emotional story set in a post-war Japan and its incredible special effects, all on a budget under US$20 million.

Much like its predecessor, Godzilla Minus Zero excels in all of those areas while also expanding on the lore of the iconic Kaiju. Minus Zero isn’t as tight as Minus One, and it isn’t quite as personal, instead focusing on a larger scale and bigger battles.

While it comes in second place when comparing the two films, the bar Minus One set was so high that even coming close to its quality is a feat worth celebrating.

From a story perspective, the standout was the introduction of Kanji. As a survivor of the atomic bomb and Godzilla, he is a deeply troubled and tormented man. His resentment towards the Americans and his obsession with researching the massive monsters easily make him the most compelling character in the entire film.

In an ideal world, Min Tanaka should be nominated for a Best Supporting Actor Oscar come award season.

The special effects here are also just as incredible as Minus One. Sequences involving fighter planes and the final battle are truly awe-inspiring, and they put to shame Hollywood blockbusters that spend 10 to 15 times the budget and somehow look worse.

Minus Zero’s score is also fantastic. Those familiar with the classic Godzilla ‘Dum dum dummmmm’ won’t miss out, while Naoki Sato’s new list of sweeping orchestral tracks more than deserves a spot on a Spotify playlist.

There are criticisms to be had, however.

Several scenes are set at a war orphanage throughout the film, and each time the narrative returns to this location, it feels out of place. It builds to a very emotional scene in the movie’s conclusion, but aside from that single scene, it feels like an afterthought.

Some of the lore expansions don’t always land either, particularly the explanation of how some people survived the attack in the first film.

The introduction of the Americans also feels slightly out of place. The Japanese reaction to Americans is fantastic, but the American characters and the depiction of their military do feel very one-note and moustache-twirling.

It would have been great to spend a few extra minutes building a realistic distrust between the two countries.

All these factors combine for a very entertaining monster flick. While Minus Zero doesn’t quite reach the heights of Minus One, I would still much rather rewatch it than any of the American films.

Godzilla Minus Zero is showing in cinemas across the country. Check showtime information for subtitle and dubbing information.

canberra.title: Two Canberra Woolworths stores to trial facial recognition technology
canberra.snippet: A trial has been proposed to fit Woolworths stores in Gungahlin and Woden with facial recognition technology to identify people who enter...
canberra.content:
Woden Woolworths will be one of two Canberra stores that are set to be fitted with facial recognition technology. Photo: Jarryd Rowley.

A trial has been proposed to fit Woolworths stores in Gungahlin and Woden with facial recognition technology to identify people who enter the store with Workplace Protection Orders (WPOs).

The new technology is expected to be trialled before the end of the month, with the intention of keeping supermarket workers safe amidst the growing occurrence of violent interactions involving customers.

The two stores were chosen for the trial because the ACT was the first jurisdiction in Australia to introduce WPOs. WPOs are legal orders made to prevent known individuals and repeat violent offenders from entering the stores that applied for the order.

WPOS give police greater powers to take action against offenders who breach court orders, unlike Woolworths-issued banning notices.

According to Woolworths, once customers enter either of the two stores, a camera will capture biometric information to create a temporary profile.

The profile is checked against a secure watchlist, created by an internal governance program, strictly containing offenders who have a history of violent, abusive or threatening behaviour in stores.

If a potential match is detected, two centralised support team members will validate it and confirm it to the store team.

The store leadership team follows through by making a risk-based decision in the interests of safety, such as calling local police.

If the system does not match the profile to the watchlist, the temporary profile containing biometric information will be deleted in less than a second.

In 2025, Woolworths Supermarkets recorded 6313 violent, abusive or threatening incidents, with 30 per cent of incidents involving known or repeat offenders.

A Canberra Woolworths staff member, who has chosen to remain anonymous, welcomed the new technology because they know several colleagues who have been attacked.

“Customers who have previously been aggressive or threatening have always been banned from the store, but to enforce that ban it has required the managers who recognise that person to be in the store at the time they try to enter,” they said.

“Facial recognition software can alert any manager in the store to the presence of a known offender. As long as the software is accurate, this will help me feel safer working at Woollies.”

Woolworths’ Head of Violence Prevention Sarah Faorlin said the treatment Woolworths team members continue to face is appalling, with unprovoked violence only becoming more common.

“Our team members are your daughters, sons, brothers, sisters, mums and your dads. We will exhaust every avenue to ensure our team members come home safe at the end of the day,” she said

“While Workplace Protection Orders (WPOs) in the ACT have proven effective, assessing the merits of facial recognition technology in-store is another way we can help protect team members and customers.

“The proposed trial of this technology will target known repeat violent, abusive or threatening offenders, including those served by court-ordered WPOs in the ACT, whose behaviour has caused a 460 per cent increase in unacceptable incidents since 2020.”

Woolworths said it will have strict privacy safeguards in place and clear signage at both stores to alert customers to the trial, which is expected to commence in late November.

canberra.title: Is the local video store due for return?
canberra.snippet: The garish patterned carpets and fluorescently lit lifesize cardboard cutouts of our favourite stars. The family challenge of choosing tw...
canberra.content:
The ritual of choosing a movie used to be as valuable as watching it. Photo: Daniella Jukic, We Are Found.

The garish patterned carpets and fluorescently lit lifesize cardboard cutouts of our favourite stars. The family challenge of choosing two new releases and five weeklies. The dodgy ”adult” section you feign disinterest in as you shuffle past.

Blockbuster, Video Ezy, Civic Video. Our mid-’90s happy places.

In Chisholm, I still remember when our local video store was revamped into a glorious Video 2000. Yes, we thought. The future is here.

Of course, with it came broadband internet, file sharing, movie piracy — and eventually, Netflix. Silent assassins, every one. Working together, they brought a quick death to our humble video store.

But recently, I have heard rumblings.

As youth culture increasingly seeks to shake off the shackles of tech addiction (clever clogs), some are longing for the simplicity of the video store.

As one meme points out (yes, memes are one of my sources — I did say rumblings), if we still need to pay $5 to rent a 30-year-old movie on one platform when we already have about three other subscription services, perhaps this is not progress. Maybe it’s preferable to simply spend 30 minutes wandering aisles, perusing DVD sleeves and selecting snacks.

Wasn’t that part of the fun, anyway?

They were simpler times — when a laminated piece of paper was all the authentification you needed. Photo: Numbskull Archives.

A trip to the video store used to be a planned event. It was part of movie night. The decision-making felt fun and exciting. It was also cooperative and done at a casual pace.

Fast-forward to today, and choosing a movie on Netflix feels like a slow-burn panic attack. One person is in charge of the remote, while the others are tasked with yelling unhelpfully: ‘’Up! Down! NO, NOT THAT ONE!’’ On the whole, not a wholesome experience and my least-favourite part of movie night.

I happened to work at one of Canberra’s last remaining video stores, a bloody great job for a struggling uni kid who grew up on Clerks and Empire Records.

We watched movies, chatted about them, cruised IMDB on the computer and occasionally vacuumed the floor. It was a vibe — and so were the customers.

It was around 2008 and Leading Edge in Belconnen was still bustling on a Friday night.

I remember comfortable old couples, nervous new couples, gaggling groups of friends and wholesome families, all happily roaming the aisles, excited to unwind together with a movie. It was an experience shared with intention.

As with most things “back in the day”, it also involved a bit of patience.

The pilgrimage to the video store was a planned event. A quest you embarked on together.

Once in the hallowed halls, you spent time reading back covers, comparing choices and making careful selections. On the way home, everyone discussed snacks and seating. At home, you changed into your comfies, settled into your spot and finally … pressed play.

Movie night was a whole multi-step thing. Consuming content, its pinnacle.

And while streaming services seem to offer an endless selection, I believe they limit our horizons. When you’ve invested time, energy and money into retrieving a specific film, it has to be pretty damned bad to warrant turning off. Basically, if you weren’t that into it, you watched it anyway.

Nowadays, with streaming services’ recommendations, ratings, reviews and previews, you have to work hard to choose a movie outside your tastes.

I know if my kids aren’t enjoying themselves immediately, they move on with the press of a button. Skipping off to a new movie is too convenient. Why should anyone push through discomfort or suspense? Or sit a little longer with something outside their typical interests?

Overall, I’d say we lost more than we bargained for when we blew off the “inconvenient” trip to the video store.

So, is it time to be kind, rewind? If your local video store reopened tomorrow, would you ditch your streaming subscription and pick up a membership card?

canberra.title: The Newcastle duo behind Oh My Papa are amping up the fun on Bunda Street
canberra.snippet: In one of the most creative uses of space in hospitality history, the Canberra Centre has retrofitted a restaurant into the hallway-like ...
canberra.content:
Fun cocktails are a big part of the Oh My Papa concept. Photo: The Canberra Centre.

In one of the most creative uses of space in hospitality history, the Canberra Centre has retrofitted a restaurant into the hallway-like space that once housed an escalator.

Spread over two floors, Oh My Papa opened in mid-October. Despite a slight delay with its alcohol licence, which forced the venue to open ‘dry’, Oh My Papa is in full swing, giving people a view of the city they haven’t previously had access to.

Part of the view from Oh My Papa’s windows is of the 10-storey, 238-room hotel opening on the Canberra Centre’s doorstep in 2027, likely the motivating factor behind squeezing a new venue into a previously utilitarian space.

In recent years, the Canberra Centre has sparked widespread industry hubbub over its tactic of enticing large hospitality groups with no local connections to fill its tenancies, and while the Oh My Papa team aren’t Canberra locals, the Humble Group, which hails from Newcastle, is far from a faceless corporation.

Oh My Papa’s moo ping pork skewers are tender and smoky. Photo: Tenele Conway.

Before The Humble Group was formed in 2021, there was just a single Thai restaurant opened by Nikki Lertaromrat and Wirat Pattanakajorn, on King Street in Newcastle, called The Humble Thai. This grew to two restaurants with the opening of The Grateful Thai in 2020, and then three venues in 2021 with the Newcastle iteration of Oh My Papa.

“It was never a plan to build a hospitality group from the beginning. It started with a passion for food, a love of hospitality and a desire to create places where people could enjoy good food and feel welcome,” Nikki tells Region.

Nikki explains that as the business grew and they explored the personalities and purpose behind each restaurant, their ambitions grew with it.

“For me, growth is not just about opening more restaurants; it is about creating something meaningful, building a strong team and giving people more reasons to come together over food.”

The Hat Yai chicken wings leverage Thailand’s legendary chicken wing town in the far south. Photo: Tenele Conway.

For Nikki, the name The Humble Group is a reminder of where they started and what really matters.

“Hospitality is an industry where success is never achieved alone. Behind every restaurant are the people who work hard every day, the customers who choose to dine with us, and the suppliers and partners who help us bring our ideas to life. We never want to take any of that for granted.”

Nikki describes Oh My Papa as having a playful personality, bringing together Asian-inspired food, cheeky cocktails, bold design, neon lights and an atmosphere that encourages people to relax, connect and have fun.

“We want dining to feel like an experience rather than simply coming in to eat and leave.”

Oh My Papa goes hard on the fusion with the tokbokki pad sieu. Photo: Tenele Conway.

With four restaurants now in the portfolio, Nikki feels the venue’s personality is just as important as the food.

“We want people to walk through the doors and immediately feel the energy, colourful, confident, a little cheeky and never boring.”

The menu is as un-boring as the space and boldly embraces a fusion experience that melds tradition and unexpected flavours. There’s a yakitori menu that, while named in the Japanese tradition, veers across Asian flavours, like the Thai moo ping pork skewers.

The small plates menu similarly hops around, focusing on fun flavour combos. You’ve got the more traditional chicken wings from Hat Yai in Thailand alongside Chinese-inspired Szechuan prawn dumplings with black vinegar and chilli, and Korean karaage chicken bao buns.

The main menu takes fusion a step further, blending cuisines on one plate, like the tokbokki pad sieu, which melds Korean rice noodles with a Thai stir-fry, or crispy squid with black ink and a South American chimichurri sauce.

Nikki links the fun cocktails to her restaurant concept of women’s empowerment. Photo: Tenele Conway.

Nikki explains that the cocktail menu is a big part of the Oh My Papa concept and hopes women will find the space empowering, feel free to laugh loudly, and be comfortable with who they are.

“In many Asian cultures, women are often expected to be polite, reserved and mindful of how they are perceived. There is nothing wrong with those qualities, but I believe women should also have the freedom to be bold, cheeky, adventurous and enjoy life on their own terms.”

Oh My Papa is located at 148 Bunda Street. They’re open 7 days a week for lunch and dinner.

canberra.title: A name like a photocopier, but a definite bargain. Why is this cut-price SUV flying under the radar?
canberra.snippet: Unless you’ve been living under a rock all year, you’ll no doubt be aware that Australia is currently facing a cost-of-living crisis. Aft...
canberra.content:
15 November 2026

Join the conversation

1

Is this budget-friendly Mahindra a bargain hiding in plain sight? Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Unless you’ve been living under a rock all year, you’ll no doubt be aware that Australia is currently facing a cost-of-living crisis.

After all, the only thing the TV news can talk about right now is the cost-of-living crisis or the collapse of David Jones. Or about why the collapse of David Jones is because of the cost-of-living crisis.

You’d think, then, that people in need of a new set of wheels would flock to buy more affordable cars at a time like this – and certainly, the numbers suggest that they are.

Just not this one, it seems.

Maybe it’s because this tiny SUV has a name like a photocopier. Maybe it’s because it still has a petrol engine. Maybe because it’s one of the few cars at this end of the market that isn’t from China.

Whatever the case, this car is an absolute bargain hiding in plain sight.

Diminutive proportions also promise a diminutive price tag, with the XUV 3XO being one of the most affordable SUVs on the market right now. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

What is it?

This is the most affordable model from Indian manufacturer Mahindra, the XUV 3XO, although the one you see here is the upscale variant.

That makes this the XUV 3XO AX7L. I told you it had a name like a photocopier.

Yet it’s closer in price to a big office photocopier than most SUVs. The entry-level AX5L version normally runs out the door for $23,990 driveaway, while the AX7L is $26,990 driveaway. There’s an all-black Anniversary Model for a little extra spend, too.

However, until the end of December 2026, Mahindra will sell you 2025-built AX5L models for as little as $22,490 driveaway, increasing to $25,490 for a 2025-built AX7L like this one.

Even if it’s a technicality, that base model deal makes it the cheapest SUV you can buy in Australia right now, beating the MG ZS Vibe ($22,990 driveaway) and its chief rival, the Chery Tiggo 4 Pro ($23,990 driveaway). It’s also considerably less than the Kia Stonic or Suzuki Fronx.

That Mahindra has enough 2025-plated stock to offer such a deal says a lot about how the XUV 3XO is faring against its successful competition, though.

Mahindra doesn’t report its sales figures to the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries (FCAI), but it announced that in 2025, it sold 4653 vehicles across its entire Australian range.

By comparison, FCAI figures show the Chery Tiggo 4 Pro alone sold 20,149 units in 2025. This year, that number was already beaten by the end of October, with year-to-date sales of 22,043 units. The MG ZS isn’t too far off those marks, either.

On the surface, it’s hard to see why the Mahinda is so overlooked in comparison. It’s quite a smart-looking thing, aside from the lurid Citrine Yellow paintwork of this example.

It’s ideally sized for city driving, able to fit in any carpark with ease. The extra ride height also makes it ‘so easy to get in and out of, you know’ (one for the Top Gear tragics out there).

It isn’t spartan, either. Cars are far from the most successful part of the Mahindra empire; Mahindra’s main success is as the world’s largest tractor manufacturer by volume, but don’t think that means it feels agricultural inside.

This AX7L version has a panoramic sunroof, leatherette upholstery, a cooled glovebox, a 360-degree camera with a handy blind-spot angle, and even a Harman Kardon premium audio system.

It’s starting to sound like pretty good value now, right?

The interior is basic, which for plenty of people is perfectly fine. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

What’s it like to live with?

There’s something to be said for the relatively analogue approach Mahindra has taken with the XUV 3XO.

Almost every key function is still controlled by a physical button, but there’s still just enough tech integration.

There are two 10.25-inch screens, one for the driver’s instrument cluster and one for the infotainment display. Both displays are impressively crisp and modern in design.

What’s great is that to change the volume or temperature, you don’t have to interact with either of them. Dials and buttons, yes please! Put anyone behind the wheel of this car, and they’ll find every control exactly where they’d expect it.

That said, the downside of this car’s budget price tag is that the fit and finish leave a little to be desired. Some of the trim wasn’t as tidy as you’d like, particularly on the dashboard. The exterior passenger-side window seal seemed to be disintegrating. Even the badges on the back aren’t quite straight.

It’s also a bit of a mixed bag on the road, though highly promising for how well suited it is to city driving.

There's more room inside than you'd think, and it's nicer than you might expect at this price – particularly with the AX7L's panoramic sunroof. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

This blind-spot camera is a handy feature, although the image resolution isn't the greatest. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

There are some signs of questionable build quality. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

And here are more signs of questionable build quality. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Powered by a tiny 1.2-litre three-cylinder engine, mercifully fitted with a turbocharger, its 85 kW power output is meagre, though 200 Nm of torque is handy.

It’s no surprise Mahindra doesn’t quote a 0-100 km/h time, although it does quote how quickly it gets from 0-60 km/h: 4.6 seconds. That tells you exactly what this car is suited to.

Like all three-cylinder engines, it has plenty of character and makes a nice thrum. It can definitely get moving at city speeds, but runs out of puff pretty quickly beyond that.

There might be three drive modes with funny names – Zip, Zap, and Zoom – but none make much of a difference either way.

The six-speed automatic transmission is a bit of a highlight, though, being a brand-name Aisin unit which performs excellently. It’s a shame the same can’t be said about its suspension, as its rudimentary torsion-beam rear suspension somewhat spoils an otherwise decent drive.

Still, were you really expecting the ultimate driving machine for this tiny sum? It’s perfectly serviceable as a city runabout, which is all it really needs to be.

The styling is a lot smarter than the price tag might suggest. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Look close enough and you may spot some crooked letters. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Look close enough and you may spot some crooked letters. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

This tiny, turbocharged three-pot packs plenty of character like most engines of its type. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

Photo: Patrick Jackson.

The verdict

Although the XUV 3XO is far from perfect, it’s quite surprising to me that I haven’t seen more of them out on the road – and that’s after spending time across most Australian cities in the past year.

What it lacks in build quality, it makes up for with simplicity and value. If you just want a car to be a car – here you are, your answer.

All I hear from people these days are complaints about how complex many modern cars are getting, from the overbearing safety systems that are hard to switch off through to the lack of clearly marked buttons.

The buttons here are big, and it’s easy to figure out which ones turn any beeps and bongs off – not that it beeps and bongs as much as many new cars.

For the sort of customers who turned to the old Mitsubishi ASX for well over a decade, this is one of the few true modern equivalents.

Quite simply, it’s four metres of car. Simple, straightforward, shameless. There’s nothing wrong with that.

Simple, straightforward, shameless… and small. Photo: Patrick Jackson.

2026 Mahindra XUV 3XO AX7L

  • $26,990 driveaway ($25,490 driveaway for 2025-built models)
  • 1.2-litre turbocharged three-cylinder, 135 kW / 244 Nm
  • Six-speed automatic, front-wheel drive
  • 6.5 litres per 100 km, 42-litre fuel capacity
  • 1410 kg kerb weight

Thanks to Mahindra Automotive Australia for providing this vehicle for testing. Region has no commercial arrangement with Mahindra Automotive Australia.

australia.content:
As Victorians vote in the state election this month, the cost of living, healthcare, housing and more are high on people’s minds.

Labor, the Coalition, the Greens and One Nation all have their ideas on how to tackle a range of pressing issues – so just what exactly are the parties promising to do if they win?

It’s important to note that not all election promises have been costed and some of the cost estimates provided by the parties have not been independently verified.

Here’s what we know about key promises across major policy areas.

australia.title: Gender-diverse Australian sailors barred from US submarines despite Aukus deal, documents reveal
australia.snippet: Defence briefing released under freedom of information laws shows ADF beholden to US directives when in training Get our breaking news em...
australia.content:
Aukus is effectively forcing the Australian navy to comply with a US ban on transgender people in the military with gender-diverse navy recruits prevented from starting a career in nuclear submarines because they would not be safe training on US boats.

Internal Australian defence force documents show transgender and non-binary sailors and officers are explicitly banned from Australia’s nuclear submarine training program because of US policies..

An internal defence briefing, released under freedom of information laws, said while ADF policy on equality and inclusion was unchanged, “US government policy is different”.

“ADF personnel undertaking duty in the US (including training) are required to comply with US policy,” the briefing said.

“Consequently, transgender and nonbinary ADF personnel and ADF career applicants are currently unable to commence the SSN [nuclear-powered attack submarines] training pathway.”

Australia, without a nuclear submarine fleet of its own, has hundreds of sailors and officers training on US nuclear submarines and on US bases.

At a women in defence event in October, Rear Adm Tish van Stralen was asked how the defence force was “managing the recruitment of gender-diverse and LGBTQ+ Australians into the nuclear submarine pathway” given the US directive.

Van Stralen, one of the highest-ranking women in the Australian navy, said the ADF was a diverse and equal opportunity employer.

But she said potential recruits for the nuclear submarine program were told the ADF was “subject to policies and laws in other countries, so we have to be very mindful”.

“We also have an obligation, a duty of care to our people, so we do not want to put our people into any sort of harm’s way or anything that might adversely affect them.

“I’m working very closely with navy at the moment and with the submarine agency around the training opportunities because it would be very difficult for me to put a gender-diverse person into that training at the moment.”

Van Stralen said the navy would seek alternative career paths for gender-diverse recruits prohibited from the nuclear submarine program. She said the UK, Australia’s other Aukus partner, had “more liberal policies” and that training opportunities “may arise in the UK”.

“We don’t want to disadvantage people because of it but we are subject to the laws and policies of the US when we are in their country.”

US moves came amid Aukus deal

The US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, last year issued a directive to his department “to eliminate all diversity, equity and inclusion offices and initiatives”. He also has sought to ban transgender personnel from joining the US military – repeatedly using offensive slurs in public statements – and ordered that transgender personnel be purged from the services.

Donald Trump signed an executive order in January 2025 – the first week of his second term as president – which banned transgender service personnel and said gender-diverse people were unfit to serve.

Announcing military cuts in September amid continued attacks on diversity, Hegseth declared that the US military would accept “no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals”.

Under the Aukus deal, it is proposed that Australia will buy three Virginia-class nuclear submarines from the US, beginning in 2032. In the lead-up to that, Australian sailors are training onboard US Virginia-class submarines and at US bases, while US-flagged nuclear submarines are porting in Australia.

Crewing Australia’s proposed nuclear submarine fleet is likely to prove one of the Aukus agreement’s most critical, sustained challenges. Virginia-class submarines have a complement of 135, more than double the crew for Australia’s diesel-electric Collins-class submarines.

Last week Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles, said the Aukus timeline presented the country with a significant “training challenge”.

“We just need to be training more people and that’s what we’re doing,” Marles said at HMAS Stirling, the West Australian port through which US nuclear-powered submarines have been rotating.

The Australian defence department did not respond to questions from the Guardian about the impact of adhering to the US policy directive, including how many Australian service personnel have been prevented from undertaking nuclear submarine training.

The government’s nuclear-powered submarine workforce strategy urges defence to “proactively expand the talent pool through active inclusion of underrepresented groups, including women, First Nations Australians, regional communities, and individuals who may not traditionally see themselves in technical or defence-related careers”.

australia.title: The Queensland ebike scheme keeping regional riders off the road: ‘If you live north of Rockhampton, bad luck’
australia.snippet: New requirements ban electric bikes that have not been assessed at a registered retailer – of which there are only nine in the state Get ...
australia.content:
An ebike has saved Queensland mother Rhianna Steindl thousands of dollars in petrol and other vehicle running costs.

In the six years since she bought her large cargo bike, it has became a common sight in her regional town of Bundaberg. Steindl often used it to commute to work, take the kids to school and more, giving up her car despite a lack of cycling infrastructure.

But a new law will probably prevent Steindl and other regional ebike users from being able to use their legal bikes.

Under new legislation passed by the Queensland state government earlier this year, e-vehicles are banned from use in public if they don’t meet a new standard capping their power at 250 watts.

Steindl says her ebike meets all the new requirements of the Electrically Power-Assisted Cycle (EPAC) assurance scheme but one: it doesn’t have the sticker that demonstrates it has been assessed at a bike retailer under the state’s new assurance scheme.

The state government quietly announced the scheme on 2 November. Just nine bike shops across the state have signed up.

Steindl’s nearest is 287km away in Rockhampton, the most northerly assurance location in the state. Owners have until just February to get their bike checked, at a capped cost of $70.

Active transport groups claim the scheme has become just the latest rushed feature of a crackdown they say has been done on the cheap and not properly thought through. They warn it risks ending the state’s e-vehicle revolution and forcing people back behind the wheel of a car.

‘This is a fiscal question’

Matt Burke, the CEO of Bikes Queensland, estimates that between 20,000 and 50,000 legal ebike across the state don’t have a sticker. He owns one of them.

A recent university of Queensland study backs this up. According to the study published last month, there are about 1m e-vehicles in the state, a fleet worth about $2.2bn.

Dr Richard Buning, the study’s author, estimates that there are 200,000 or more “legal” vehicles in the state that need a sticker.

Ebikes aren’t just common in the cities. A third of Queensland households own an e-mobility device, including about 28% of households in remote Queensland, the study found.

Burke said most big retailers have already declined to be part of the scheme because it isn’t worth their while and is labor intensive.

“This is a fiscal question. The government has chosen not to fund this appropriately, that’s what’s happened,” he said.

He said there will be no way for owners in most owners in regional Queensland to get their vehicle accredited before an enforcement grace period runs out.

“If you live north of Rockhampton, bad luck,” he said. “There’s going to be no one within almost 700km of some of these cities, like Cairns and Townsville, where you can get your bike verified.

“So not the greatest outcome of a government service scheme.”

Some ebike owners argue that the Christmas holidays may complicate the scheme even further, given that, for many shops, it’s the busiest time of year.

Others are questioning why service centres operated by the Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR)are not participating, given that they already do vehicle inspections for cars virtually everywhere in the state.

Peter Bourke, the general manager of Bicycle Industries Australia, said they are working with TMR to expand the scheme’s coverage across Queensland “very rapidly”, though it won’t be universal.

“We will be increasing the number of stores online. I’m hoping by the end of the month there will be 20 stores, with further stores in the new year that will be able to undertake verifications,” he said.

He said an assessment will take about half an hour to complete, so there should be no capacity problem. Bike shops were chosen as the delivery arm because they already had the skills, which TMR service centres do not, he said.

The TMR website says “alternative arrangements” will be available for those who live in a rural or remote area without reasonable access to an authorised verifier, “including the potential for a temporary, conditional permit”. It promises an update early next year. There are no further details available.

The only alternative

Like most of the world’s transport agencies, Queensland’s says it aims to encourage more people to give up their car and ride.

According to the Queensland Cycling Strategy 2017-2027, active transport “can reduce traffic congestion and have many health benefits for those who choose to cycle”, reduces the state’s carbon footprint and saves the state government money.

The department particularly commits to encouraging “active school travel” and to prioritise “people who need more support to start riding such as children, women and older people”, because they are the least likely to already cycle.

But Buning said the legislation risks undermining progress towards those goals.

He said ebike technology had had a “transformative” effect in Europe and Asia, proving to be a remarkably effective tool for shifting people out of a car, substantially increasing cycling rates – disproportionately among more vulnerable users – because ebikes don’t require as much physical fitness.

“The real benefit of e-mobility devices is it’s made active transport that more attractive to just so much wider a segment of the population,” he said.

“There’s nothing in my time of researching this space for nearly two decades that’s encouraged people to want to use active transport as much.”

Queensland’s legislation targets exactly the groups the department wants to encourage to cycle, banning children under 16 and many old people from riding an e-vehicle at all. The first draft of the legislation would have also banned much of the state’s disabled community, but was amended to provide a medical exemption.

According to the law’s explanatory note, it was designed to force e-vehicle riders away from almost all of Brisbane’s safe cycling network into general traffic – which Buning said would also discourage female riders, who are known to be less risk averse.

The government-dominated Queensland parliamentary committee, which recommended the legislation, heard that there is no evidence of any public safety risk associated with legal ebikes. It identified just a single fatal accident involving a legal ebike during its year-long inquiry, an elderly woman killed by a car.

Buning’s research shows that, for a quarter of the state’s e-mobility users, a private car is their only alternative, particularly in regional areas.

“If you live in one of those areas, you have no access to public transport. You have no other access way of getting around.”

Burke said the scheme had been rushed and not properly thought through. Queensland is falling behind the rest of the world, he said.

“Queensland is slow on the adoption of e-mobility and of cycling more generally,” he said.

“New York has just tripled in recent years, Paris has multiplied it by about seven times. London has had really steep increases.

“We’re not in a good space in Queensland. We will be even more behind where everyone else in the world is headed.”

A spokesperson for Transport and Main Roads said the scheme is “already helping Queenslanders retain and use eligible devices safely and legally”.

“Authorised verification locations are now operating across the state and more locations are expected to come online in the coming weeks,” they said.

Steindl says she has given up riding the ebike as a result of the legislation and instead drives her four-wheel drive everywhere. Diesel is now among her highest household bills.

“You know what? It’s just easier to get in the car,” she said.

australia.title: How sensitive data from Centrelink and other Australian agencies may have been fed to Palantir software
australia.snippet: Exclusive: Personal information of Centrelink clients and childcare workers is among data shared with ACIC, which uses US tech company’s ...
australia.content:
The personal information of Centrelink customers, taxpayers and childcare workers is among a trove of sensitive data that may be ending up in Palantir’s surveillance software in Australia, without the departments responsible for the information even knowing about it.

As Guardian Australia reported in September, Palantir’s software is used by the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC) as part of the multi-agency fraud fusion taskforce, which was established in 2022 with the goal of targeting fraud in government payments from the national disability insurance scheme, childcare and welfare.

New documents, released under freedom of information requests, reveal the extent to which at least 10 government agencies share sensitive data with the taskforce, which could be fed into Palantir’s software.

The controversial US tech company, co-founded by the Donald Trump-aligned billionaire Peter Thiel, has clients including the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that use the software to analyse vast amounts of data.

While the company has insisted it has no access to the data clients enter into the software, the Greens leader, David Shoebridge, has led calls for a ban on Palantir contracts with the Australian government.

In April, the company implied some cultures were inferior to others in a 22-point manifesto posted on X and described by one UK MP as the “ramblings of a supervillain”. Shoebridge has said Palantir should not be near Australian data given how the data mining software is used by the IDF and ICE.

The Australian government has spent nearly $80m on Palantir contracts since May.

A data-sharing network

The taskforce is headed up by the National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIA) and Services Australia. The intelligence program – known as the fraud fusion centre – is led by the ACIC, and brings in “large volumes of information, data and intelligence” held by agencies that could be relevant to the taskforce work, according to the documents released under FoI.

The FoI requests, undertaken by Dr Gabrielle Josling, an independent researcher and data scientist, showed at least 10 federal agencies were sharing data with the ACIC – data that could ultimately be put in Palantir’s software by the commission.

Documents from the Department of Education show the ACIC is “collecting criminal intelligence and analysing and crossmatching data” from sources including:

  • The education department.

  • The NDIA.

  • Services Australia.

  • The NDIS Quality Safeguards Commission.

  • The Australian Taxation Office.

  • Australian federal police.

  • The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (Asic).

  • The Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre.

  • The health department.

  • The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations.

The personal information authorised by Services Australia to be obtained by the ACIC includes names, date of birth, information about proof of ID, addresses, telephone numbers, Centrelink claims or reviews, itemised income and asset details, employer information, bank account information and “surveillance material” held by the agency.

The collected data is held by the fraud fusion centre and, while a privacy impact assessment noted that the ACIC is not subject to the Privacy Act, the agency’s protocols state it acts in accordance with the Australian privacy principles “wherever reasonably consistent with the effective performance of its statutory functions”.

Services Australia said each disclosure to the ACIC was considered on a case-by-case basis. There had been two disclosures in the financial year to date, compared with 21 in 2025-26 and 47 in 2024-25.

The ATO’s documents do not reveal the extent of the data provided by the agency but state that tax file numbers cannot be provided under law. It made 758 disclosures between November 2022 and July 2026, including 376 to the NDIA and 42 to the ACIC.

A spokesperson for the ATO told Guardian Australia the taxpayer information was disclosed where it was “lawfully able” to do so under the terms of the memorandum of understanding as part of the taskforce, the ATO’s intelligence disclosure governance plan and the Tax Administration Act.

The federal education department has withheld releasing information about what data it has provided to the taskforce but the documents state it is data related to the childcare subsidy scheme.

A spokesperson for the department refused to comment on “detailed operational information-sharing arrangements” and directed questions about Palantir use to the ACIC.

The ACIC said data handling is subject to agreements with the agency supplying the data, and that Palantir was “part of a suite of analytical tools to undertake analysis on specific cases to assist partner agencies to disrupt serious organised crime networks defrauding government programs”.

The agency did not respond to questions from Guardian Australia on whether other federal agencies were informed if the data provided was ingested into Palantir’s software. Neither the ATO nor Centrelink were aware if Palantir was used.

“The use of software by another agency is a question for that agency, and any questions relating to ACIC use of data obtained under the FFT are best directed to the ACIC,” an ATO spokesperson said.

‘Guide’ replaced ethics framework

The documents reveal that the memorandum of understanding in 2024 between taskforce agencies originally required the taskforce to develop an ethics and human oversight framework governing the control of the information shared. It was described as “an important part of effective risk management for the FFT”.

Ethical risks were supposed to be assessed and recorded on a risks register.

But correspondence released from September 2025 reveal that it was determined that the process was “too difficult to implement” and the framework instead became an “ethics guide” in October last year.

In a submission to the Australian National Audit Office calling for a review into the taskforce, Josling said the new model abandoned requirements for defined assessments and reviews of the taskforce. A framework for evaluating and monitoring the performance of the taskforce was also not developed.

“A multi-agency taskforce needs a way to learn from data quality problems, data matching limitations, unproductive referrals, emerging risks, and weaknesses in governance,” Josling said in the submission.

Companies and governments have faced pressure to stop using Palantir, with both Coles and Westpac reportedly deciding against renewing their contracts with the firm. The UK government has also faced pressure to drop its contracts with Palantir, including a contract with the NHS.

Palantir has maintained that it does not have access to the data clients enter into its software. A spokesperson has previously defended the company’s contracts with the Australian government, saying it is just a software company.

“We are committed to supporting Australian government agencies in tackling complex challenges, including serious financial crime and fraud,” they said.

world.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
world.snippet: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-...
world.content:
The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”

She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.

Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.

Associated Press contributed to this report

world.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
world.snippet: Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent Lewis Hamilton has visited Egyp...
world.content:
Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.

Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.

At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.

The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.

The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

world.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
world.snippet: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and...
world.content:
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.

The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment.

Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.

Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.

Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died, he said.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

Outside al-Wasta central hospital in Beni Suef province, where some of the injured were taken for treatment, survivors said passengers were in shock and struggling to breathe because of all the dust that was kicked up. Nearby villagers eventually got them out, they said.

Farha Gamal, a survivor who was inside the Fayyoum train, said she saw some of the passengers who appeared dead and others were struggling to find their way out of the car. “There were other cars that were completely mangled,” she said in an interview.

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the crash site to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002 when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

world.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
world.snippet: See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and...
world.content:
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.

See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.

The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.

“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”

Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”

See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

world.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
world.snippet: Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families The l...
world.content:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.

In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.

Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Reuters contributed reporting
